origin_region: Hubei · Yichang (Wuling mountains, incl. Hunan Shimen)
cultivar: Local Wuling-mountain medium-leaf population bushes and Yichang selections
processing: Fully oxidised gongfu black: withered, rolled, oxidised in warm rooms and dried, then sorted and graded by leaf size and tip.
harvest_season: Spring (April) for the main harvest; summer and early autumn pickings go into the lower grades.
appearance_dry: Tight, slim, dark strands with a sprinkling of golden tips and a slight sheen.
appearance_liquor: Bright red, clouding as it cools – the 'cold cloudiness' makers point to as a quality sign.
appearance_wet: Even copper-red leaves, soft and whole.
taste_profile: Sweet and mellow with malt, dried fruit and a honeyed finish, medium body and a soft tannin that suits milk.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan at 90–95 °C, short steeps. Western-style: 3 g per 250 ml, 3 minutes; good with milk.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest, graded by tip content, mostly within Hubei and through a few export channels; drink within a year or two. Not aged.
description:
Yi Hong is the gongfu black of the Wuling mountains along the Hubei–Hunan border, named after Yichang on the Yangtze, the port it was shipped from. It dates from the mid-nineteenth century, when Cantonese merchants set up black-tea making in the hills of Yidu, Wufeng, Hefeng and Changyang for the Hankou export trade, and by the end of the century it was one of the big names in Chinese congou alongside Keemun and Ningchow.

The tea is made in the standard gongfu way from the medium-leaf mountain bushes – withering, rolling, oxidation in warm rooms, drying, sorting – and it comes out a shade heavier than the Fujian blacks. Local makers point to 'cold cloudiness', the way a strong cup turns milky as it cools, as the mark of a good Yi Hong; it is a sign of plenty of the compounds that give body and colour.

In the cup expect malt and dried fruit with a honeyed sweetness, medium body and a soft tannin that does not bite; six or seven short steeps at around 92 °C, or a three-minute pot that takes milk well. It is a breakfast-weight tea with a gentler edge than an Assam.

It is sold as the current spring, graded by tips, mostly within Hubei and through a few traders; the Yidu and Wufeng names carry the most weight locally. Look for tight, even, slightly tippy leaf and a sweet, malty dry aroma, and treat 'Yi Hong' on tea from far outside the Wuling hills as a style claim rather than an origin.

If you want a Chinese black for milk that is not Yingde, this and Hu Hong from the next province are the ones to try.
sources_note: Mid-19th-century origin and the Hankou export role are the standard Chinese tea-history account. 'Ichang' is the historical trade spelling. The Hunan Shimen inclusion in the production area follows Chinese sources.
